epithet: al-Farisi (The Persian), Ibn al-Islam (Son of Islam)
tribe: Persian (from Isfahan, Persia); no Arab tribal affiliation
role: Proposer of the trench at the Battle of al-Khandaq
summary: Salman al-Farisi (RA) was a Persian companion of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ whose life story is one of the most extraordinary in Islamic history: a decades-long spiritual journey from Zoroastrianism through Christianity, from Persia to Syria to Iraq to Arabia, driven by a relentless search for truth. His suggestion to dig a trench at the Battle of al-Khandaq was a strategic masterstroke. The Prophet ﷺ declared him to be 'of the family of the Prophet,' and his Persianness is specifically cited in a narration about the spread of Islam beyond the Arabs.
biography:
Salman al-Farisi (RA) was born in Isfahan (or the village of Jayy near Isfahan), Persia, around 568 CE into a prominent Zoroastrian family. His father was the village's dehqan (landowner-administrator) and a devout Zoroastrian fire-keeper. Salman, given the name Ruzbeh in his youth, was groomed to take over his father's role. The detailed account of his spiritual journey is preserved in narrations compiled by Ibn Hisham in al-Seerah al-Nabawiyyah and Ibn Sa'd in al-Tabaqat al-Kubra, reportedly from Salman's own telling to the Companions. (The detailed personal narrative is a well-known seerah account; its chain of transmission is discussed by hadith scholars, and it is treated as a historical narrative rather than a formally graded hadith.)

Salman's search began when, as a young man entrusted with tending his family's land, he happened to pass a Christian church and was moved by the prayers he heard inside. He entered, listened, and was profoundly affected — more so than he had ever been by Zoroastrian ritual. He began attending the church secretly, informing his father, who was distressed and locked him in the house. Salman eventually escaped to Syria, where he became a student of a Christian bishop he considered the most sincere man of God he had encountered. That bishop died and, on his deathbed, directed Salman to another scholar in Mosul, who in turn directed him to another in Nisibis, who in turn directed him to another in Ammuriyyah (in Anatolia). Each scholar, at death, directed him forward.

The last of these Christian guides told him that he knew of a prophet who would appear in the land of the Arabs, who would eat gifted food but not alms (sadaqah), and between whose shoulder blades would be a seal of prophethood. He told Salman to seek this prophet. Salman traveled toward Arabia with a group of Arab traders but was seized and enslaved by them, eventually sold to a Jewish man of the Banu Qurayza in Madinah. This slaveholder later sold him to another man of the Banu Qayla.

When the Prophet ﷺ arrived in Madinah in 1 AH (622 CE), Salman heard the news and came to observe him. He confirmed two of the three signs: the Prophet ﷺ ate gifted food but refused sadaqah. Then, when Salman glimpsed the seal of prophethood between the Prophet's ﷺ shoulder blades, he reportedly wept and immediately declared the shahada. The Prophet ﷺ asked him to share his story, and the account was told to the Companions, becoming one of the most celebrated conversion narratives in Islamic tradition.

The Prophet ﷺ helped Salman secure his freedom through a manumission agreement (mukataba) with his master, requiring him to plant a specified number of date palms and produce a certain amount of gold. The Companions and the Prophet ﷺ himself helped: the Prophet ﷺ planted sixty-nine or seventy of the palm saplings with his own hands. All the trees took root, and the gold requirement was later met. Salman was free.

Salman's most impactful contribution came at the Battle of al-Khandaq (5 AH / 627 CE), when the Quraysh formed an enormous coalition — estimated by classical sources at ten thousand fighters — to besiege Madinah. Salman proposed digging a trench (khandaq) along the exposed northern approaches of Madinah, a defensive stratagem well-known in Persian warfare but unfamiliar to the Arabs. The Prophet ﷺ immediately approved and Muslims dug the trench over several days, the Prophet ﷺ himself participating. The trench neutralized the coalition's numerical and cavalry advantage. The confederate army camped outside for nearly a month and eventually withdrew. Salman was so beloved that both the Muhajirun and the Ansar competed to claim him as 'one of us,' and the Prophet ﷺ resolved it by saying: 'Salman is of the family of the Prophet (Salman minna, Ahl al-Bayt).' (al-Hakim, al-Mustadrak; Ibn Hisham, al-Seerah al-Nabawiyyah).

A well-known Quranic commentary tradition connects Salman to the meaning of Surah al-Jumu'ah 62:3, which mentions the spread of the Quran to people 'who have not yet joined them' — interpreted by many classical exegetes (including those cited in al-Tirmidhi) as referring to the Persians, with Salman as the exemplar.

After the Prophet's ﷺ death, Salman participated in the Islamic conquests. He was appointed the governor of al-Mada'in (Ctesiphon), the former Sasanian capital in Iraq, under Umar and then Uthman (RA). He governed justly and lived simply — some accounts say he lived in a rough dwelling and owned almost nothing despite governing one of the wealthiest cities of his era. He died in al-Mada'in around 35-36 AH (655-656 CE) at a very advanced age; classical sources vary between 80 and 350 years for his total lifespan, the latter being clearly exaggerated in transmission — most careful scholars like al-Dhahabi and Ibn Kathir note the uncertainty and the implausibility of extreme age claims while accepting that he was very elderly at death.

key_events.event: Left Persia, beginning decades-long search for truth — from Zoroastrianism to Christianity
Enslaved by Arab traders; sold to a man of Banu Qayla in Madinah
Prophet ﷺ arrived in Madinah; Salman confirmed the three signs and accepted Islam
Prophet ﷺ helped Salman fulfill his manumission agreement; planted date palms personally
Proposed the trench (khandaq) strategy at the Battle of al-Khandaq — decisive for the defense of Madinah
Declared by the Prophet ﷺ as 'of the family of the Prophet (Ahl al-Bayt)'
Appointed governor of al-Mada'in (Ctesiphon) by Umar ibn al-Khattab
Died in al-Mada'in at a very advanced age

notable_traits: Decades-long spiritual journey across multiple religions and countries — Islam was the destination of a genuine search for truth
Strategic genius — trench idea at al-Khandaq changed the course of Islamic history
Declared part of Ahl al-Bayt by the Prophet ﷺ despite being non-Arab
Extraordinary asceticism as governor — lived with almost nothing despite ruling a wealthy city
Symbol of Islam's universality — the Prophet ﷺ specifically associated him with Islam reaching the Persians

key_relationships.relationship_to_prophet: Adopted into the Prophet's household ('Salman minna Ahl al-Bayt')
spiritual_guides: A series of Christian bishops leading him from Persia through Syria to Anatolia

narrated_hadith_count: approximately 60 hadith in the major collections
